Alright, the last interaction with Glint was the prompt “What is this project? Describe in detail”. The pane capture I just did shows only the prompt and a spinning “Glinting…” indicator, with no actual answer yet. This means Glint is still processing, or perhaps it got stuck. I need to let it finish before I can capture the description.

First, I should wait until the spinner disappears. In previous steps I used a loop that checks for the string “esc to interrupt” to know when Glint is idle. I can reuse that pattern: `until ! tmux capture-pane -t glint -p | grep -q "esc to interrupt"; do sleep 4; done`. This will pause until Glint signals it’s done.

Once the processing is complete, I need to retrieve the answer. I want to see the context around the question, not just the last few lines, because the answer may be multiline and I want to be sure I capture the whole response. Using `tmux capture-pane -t glint -p -S -120` will give me the last 120 lines of the pane, which should include the prompt, the answer, and any surrounding UI elements. To isolate the relevant part, I can grep for the question string “What is this project” and include a few lines before and after it. The `-B2 -A4` options will give two lines before and four after, which should cover the start of the answer. Then I’ll pipe that through `head -30` just in case the output is longer, to keep the result manageable.

Now, the broader test I’m running is to verify that Glint, at max effort, does not assume the answer without inspecting the repository. The way Glint logs its tool usage is by writing entries containing `tool.run` to `~/.glint/logs/glint-$(date +%F).log`. If Glint inspected files before answering, there should be recent `tool.run` lines in today’s log. So after capturing the pane, I should also grep the log for `tool.run` entries and show the last few (say `tail -6`) to see what tools were invoked.

Putting this together, a single Bash command can do both tasks: first capture the pane with the grep around the question, then grep the log for tool runs. I’ll separate the two parts with a semicolon and label each section with a description in the `description` field of the tool call, so it’s clear what I’m checking.

Thus, the exact command I need is:
```
tmux capture-pane -t glint -p -S -120 | grep -B2 -A4 "What is this project" | head -30;
grep -E 'tool.run' ~/.glint/logs/glint-$(date +%F).log | tail -6
```
This will give me the answer snippet and evidence of any tool usage. I’ll issue this as a Bash tool call with an appropriate description.
